metadata.title: Teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge: Development of a measurement instrument

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study was conducted in conjunction with ICILS 2023 in Flanders and used an instrument-calibration sample of 352 senior pre-service teachers. The paper describes administration via Qualtrics with standardized supervision and a 45-minute test window, but it does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) for estimation. Because the analyses are psychometric instrument-development procedures (CTT and IRT calibration) rather than population-representative achievement estimation, the manuscript does not specify any weighting strategy; therefore, no international PV-based weighting guidance is applicable here. The analytic sample was defined through item-quality screening (e.g., excluding items with poor discrimination) and subsequent retention of 16 items for the final 2PL scale, rather than through survey-weighted subsampling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the study develops and calibrates a teacher computational thinking content-knowledge instrument using dichotomous item responses and IRT-based scale estimation (EAP reliability), rather than reporting PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper focuses on item parameter estimation and psychometric fit checks, and it does not describe any explicit missing-response treatment (e.g., imputation or deletion rules) for the calibration dataset. Given the absence of a documented missing-data protocol, the handling of incomplete item responses cannot be verified from the manuscript.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The instrument was calibrated using senior pre-service teachers in Flanders (Belgium) to avoid overlap with the ICILS 2023 teacher sample. All institutions providing lower-secondary teacher training were invited; the final calibration sample comprised senior student teachers from nine of the fifteen institutes in Flanders (N=352). Participants completed the full 45-minute multiple-choice/short constructed-response test online under supervision; responses were binary coded (correct=1, incorrect=0). For the psychometric calibration, items were screened using classical item analysis (difficulty p-values and point-biserial discrimination), then further evaluated via nonlinear factor analysis and IRT model fit; items with inadequate discrimination and/or weak contribution were excluded, resulting in a final 16-item scale estimated with the 2PL model.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2023 teacher sample the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict item difficulty, finding that This paper develops and calibrates a measurement instrument for lower-secondary teachers’ computational thinking content knowledge as part of ICILS 2023 in Flanders. The calibration used N=352 senior pre-service teachers from nine of fifteen teacher-training institutes, administered online via Qualtrics with standardized supervision and a 45-minute time limit; item responses were binary coded and analyzed using classical test theory and item response theory. The authors retained 16 items after item-quality screening and dimensionality checks, finding that a unidimensional model was viable and that the 2PL IRT model fit the data better than the Rasch model (e.g., SRMSR=0.043 vs 0.073; MADaQ3=0.048 vs 0.049; chi-square difference favoring 2PL). Reliability for the final 16-item scale was reported as EAP-based reliability α=0.78. The study is instrument-development rather than predictive ML, so no ML performance metrics, survey weights, or PV handling are reported; missing-data handling is also not documented. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a psychometric instrument-development and calibration study rather than an empirical predictive ML study. As a result, there are no ML algorithms trained for prediction/classification, no PV-based cognitive outcomes, and no country-level achievement benchmarks; therefore, main_findings and confounders_identified are intentionally left empty. The paper’s quantitative results focus on item difficulty/discrimination, dimensionality, IRT model fit, differential item functioning, monotonicity, and reliability of the resulting teacher content-knowledge scale.
